📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war.

Recent findings suggest that I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

Industry observers note that the woman who sent me the photo notes the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

It has been revealed that "Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it remarked.

It turned my world upside down.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

According to recent reports, now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.

The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025.

Recent findings suggest that I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

Recent findings suggest that but earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents.

Recent findings suggest that I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

Industry observers note that I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly declared the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he noted.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] noted it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family?

BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only).

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here.

Watch our YouTube documentary here, external.

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

It has been revealed that their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

According to recent reports, at this time, she stated, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones.".

According to recent reports, she said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

In a recent development, "You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina remarked they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she noted, despite the freezing conditions.

Recent findings suggest that with drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she mentioned, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too.".

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

Sources indicate that "Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The upcoming local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, remarked she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it noted his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.

He noted he did not know anything about who killed them.

Recent findings suggest that "I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial.

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, mentioned his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

According to recent reports, it stated it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

Sources indicate that however, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father.

It has been revealed that she is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place.

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

Sources indicate that "Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces.
  • Sources indicate that the central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances.
  • government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

Sources indicate that the central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.

Sources indicate that the U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.

Industry observers note that diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine problem for a firm like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end people of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.

Industry observers note that and that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the firm’s legal risk.

“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.

The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.

In a recent development, on Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued fresh rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, remarked it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.

Nvidia’s board noted it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.

In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche mentioned that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.

“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche stated.

It has been revealed that other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly, the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the organization’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.

It has been revealed that members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China stated in a joint statement.

It has been revealed that rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.

The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.

In a recent development, “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the manufacturer’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.

It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.

The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Confirming the expulsion, KCNA mentioned: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours.".

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.

Switzerland's Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis (C) and his wife Paola Cassis (R) were greeted by a North Korean official at Pyongyang Airport on 29 October.

Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine.".

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky indicates.

North Korean weapons are killing Ukrainians. The implications are far bigger.

Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine.

#116082. Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1016 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
  • In a recent development, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China.
  • The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

In a recent development, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its owners’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

In a recent development, as the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York Joseph Nocella Jr. said that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage firm called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ remarked. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ noted, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade indicates and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Newly introduced York Times reported.

In a recent development, huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ remarked was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, remarked that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the manufacturer’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

In a recent development, huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

According to recent reports, outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by company employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig noted.

After the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo mentioned.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

According to recent reports, “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky stated. “No company is too significant, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The feature is now rolling out in public beta.

WhatsApp's latest public beta release adds a latest feature that could make chatting with your friends more fun: stickers that play sounds when you tap them. You know how the chat app lets you create your own stickers, even animated ones? Well, it's pretty much the same thing, except you can also add audio. That gives you an easy way to recreate iconic video clips, such as Josh Hutcherson's Whistle edit meme, which has been making the rounds again thanks to the Sunrise on the Reaping movie.

According to recent reports, according to WABetaInfo, sound stickers are part of beta update 2.26.41.3 for Android. If you want to try it out, you can apply to become a tester for the chat app through Google Play. To make a sound sticker, open a chat, tap the sticker icon and then tap Create sticker. From there, you can choose a video from your library, which WhatsApp will automatically convert into a sticker.

Sources indicate that now, you'll find the latest Sound icon at the top menu. Tap it to open the new Add sound screen. From there, you can keep the video's original audio, record a voice note or any other custom sound you want to use, or choose an audio file saved on your phone. When you're done, you can save the sound sticker and send it to as many people as you want.

According to recent reports, since the feature is experimental, you might not be able to access it right now, even if you're already a beta tester. WhatsApp has yet to announce whether it will roll out to all owners in the future.

Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company.
  • On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found.
  • A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company.

On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found.

A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.

Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the firm’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018.

Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart stated its business grew more than five-fold. The manufacturer has more than 500 million registered customers and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories.

In a recent development, flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes. The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics.

Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile.

According to recent reports, krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the manufacturer moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first.

According to recent reports, walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO prepares. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment.

Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon.

“Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the organization,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, noted in a statement.

#116074. Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1131 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.
  • Recent findings suggest that modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home.
  • With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.

Recent findings suggest that modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet.

With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side.

Recent findings suggest that around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader.

Recent findings suggest that all told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That stated, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice.

In a recent development, the real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think.

When I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's important to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you plan on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing.

Recent findings suggest that similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That mentioned, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too.

The Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions.

It has been revealed that I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8.

At $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That said, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.

  • In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early license review for eight ABC stations, even though their licenses were not set to expire until 2028.
  • ABC sued, arguing that the move was retaliation for broadcasting content that angered President Donald Trump.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A US judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ‌from ⁠continuing ⁠to take steps that threaten ABC's ​broadcast license.

In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early license review for eight ABC stations, even though their licenses were not set to expire until 2028.

ABC sued, arguing that the move was retaliation for broadcasting content that angered President Donald Trump.

On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan noted the FCC ​chair appeared to have taken "marching orders" from Trump's rhetoric.

According to recent reports, "This is not a close case," she wrote in her ruling. "No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.".

Carr's order to review ABC's licenses had come a day after Trump called for ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he made. His show was taken off the air for six days amid pressure from the White House.

The broadcaster, which is owned by the Walt Disney Company, welcomed the ruling on Wednesday.

"Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the FCC mentioned the ruling was "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.".

"We will ​continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added.

But one dissenting opinion within the FCC came from its sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez.

She stated the ruling brought "badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control.".

Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
  • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
  • We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

According to recent reports, I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are important because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki noted:.

Unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key complications remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.

Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.

Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.

Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

A solar generator can keep devices and appliances running during a power outage or when you're off-grid. Although prices have come down in recent years, they still aren't exactly cheap. So Black Friday isn't a bad time to invest in one before winter hits.

If we're being literal, there's only one "solar generator," and that's the sun. These are just massive batteries with inputs for solar panels and outlets for all your stuff. But "solar generator" conjures the image marketers want, so that's what the industry went with.

With Black Friday sales already underway, you can save roughly 20 to 40 percent on models from top brands. The two most key specs to look at are capacity and output. Especially if you're buying one to back up your home or large appliances, make sure it has enough output to handle your device load and enough capacity to run as long as you need.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that most of these sales don't include solar panels, so you'll want to factor that into your total cost. Also, shipping for some of these models is estimated to run into mid-December or even January, so you may need to be patient. Sale prices tend to wiggle leading up to the substantial day: look closely before checking out.

The Bluetti Elite 100 V2 has a 1,024Wh capacity, an 1,800W output and 11 ports. It's right now available on Amazon for $493, a discount from its $729 list price. However, the listing is marked as non-returnable, so make sure the model is exactly what you want before pulling the trigger.

Then there's the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. It, too, has a 1,024Wh capacity, but with a 2,000W output. This model supports Anker's "UltraFast Charging," which can charge from empty to full in 49 minutes, according to the firm. (You have to turn it on in Anker's app, though, and it only works when the battery is warmer than 68 degrees Fahrenheit.) On Anker's website, it's currently marked down to $470 from its $799 MSRP.

Anker's SOLIX S2000 takes a different approach: less power at once, but twice the battery capacity. (Specifically, that's 1,500W output and 2,010Wh capacity.) It's marked down to $650 from its $1,000 list price on Anker's website. This sale is only listed through November 26, so technically this is more of a Thanksgiving sale than a Black Friday one.

If you're willing to invest in a bigger system for home backup, EcoFlow has a couple of options on sale. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 has a nearly 4kWh capacity that expands to 12kWh with extra batteries (not included), along with a 3,600W output. It's discounted on EcoFlow's website to $1,699 from its standard $2,199.

Sources indicate that finally, there's EcoFlow's TITAN 5000 Classic. It has a 5kWh capacity (expandable to 30kWh) and a 4,000W output. EcoFlow sells the standalone unit for $2,199 (down from $3,299), and a bundle that includes four 175W solar panels for $2,899 (down from $4,295).

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in Fresh York to Saturday because of severe weather.
    • Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade.

    Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in Fresh York to Saturday because of severe weather.

    Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

    According to recent reports, the last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.

    A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.

    The balloons will be deflated again and then re-inflated for Saturday.

    On Wednesday night, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for Long Island, New York City and Westchester County.

    The potent nor'easter is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.

    Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.

    "While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," remarked Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.

    Cross also noted the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring Newly introduced Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.

    Macy's confirmed the upcoming parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has noted it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.

    New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, mentioned at the news conference that "you have to initiative for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.

    Sources indicate that "We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety.".

    Mamdani also mentioned that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".

    Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and stated the tech giant is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.

    BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.

    During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.

    The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.

    Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow, BBC Weather reports.

    The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).

    Governor Mikie Sherrill's office mentioned the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.

    Industry observers note that originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.

    From 1942 to 1944 Fresh York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.

    The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.

    Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

    Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.
    • Sources indicate that todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the firm’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23.
    • Industry observers note that the hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist people whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the firm said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.

    Sources indicate that todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the firm’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.

    Industry observers note that the hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist people whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the firm said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.

    For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.

    The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.

    In a recent development, the tech giant noted it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking consumers to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.

    Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.

    Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X, and stated the company will take a closer look at why it happened.

    Industry observers note that the to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the tech giant to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

    In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

    Sources indicate that “Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

    Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the manufacturer had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

    He remarked he still plans on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

    In a recent development, “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he stated. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

    He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

    “This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

    In a recent development, the fracas began earlier this month, when the manufacturer first proposed new contractual language. The updated terms read:.

    As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

    Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account customers to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

    Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

    “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

    For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

    • SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.

    SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.

    In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

    It has been revealed that the FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

    It has been revealed that spaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It aims to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

    Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

    The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed.

    Sources indicate that the breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.).

    Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams, the airlines, Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.

    In a recent development, downdetector, a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows consumers began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.

    The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a substantial travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.

    Sources indicate that allstate did not immediately return a request for comment. On Wednesday evening, after publication, the tech giant sent the following statement (below). It did not answer questions about the outage’s cause or planned resolution.

    Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures demonstrates.

    Sources indicate that trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (Â£4m and Â£13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

    Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

    Sources indicate that the period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

    The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

    Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

    But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

    Sources indicate that trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board stated it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (Â£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the firm's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

    However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

    Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

    In a recent development, the firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable firm on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

    Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

    Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

    Trump made at least $2.2bn (Â£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

    Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency.".

    Additional reporting Becky Dale.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You’ll be able to schedule a text, photo or video message up to 14 days in advance.
    • WhatsApp is introducing what it claims is one of the most-requested features from users: scheduled messages.
    • You'll be able to schedule a WhatsApp message to send between 10 minutes and 14 days in the future.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You’ll be able to schedule a text, photo or video message up to 14 days in advance.

    WhatsApp is introducing what it claims is one of the most-requested features from users: scheduled messages. This option will be available globally in the coming weeks and it'll support text, photo and video. Sibling app Instagram has offered scheduled messages since 2024, so this is a long overdue enhancement.

    You'll be able to schedule a WhatsApp message to send between 10 minutes and 14 days in the future. Scheduled messages will work in both one-on-one conversations and group chats.

    Once the feature is available on your account, you can schedule a message by pressing and holding the send button. You'll then be able to pick a date and time to transmit your message. The recipients won't know that it's a scheduled message as it'll look like any other update to them.

    This is a very welcome feature. One of the few things I genuinely like about email (other than it being a truly decentralized means of communication) is being able to schedule replies. I don't really need anyone to know that I'm actually hashing out an email to them late at night. I usually schedule it to send the next morning so I don't seem like someone who works too much even though I definitely work too much.

    WhatsApp suggested some other ways scheduled messages might be useful, such as to wish someone luck just before a test or job interview, or to make sure they receive a happy birthday message right when it's midnight for them (especially if you're not in the same time zone). You'll be able to see all of the messages you've timed up to send in the future and delete them if you change your mind. WhatsApp said that, as with all other personal messages, scheduled messages are end-to-end encrypted, so only you and the recipient(s) can read them.
