    #116043. Tech Report: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements.
    • It has been revealed that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux.
    • In a recent development, ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.

    It has been revealed that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious consumers had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.

    In a recent development, ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”.

    Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

    According to recent reports, an independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.

    Sources indicate that the Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a latest independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

    According to recent reports, the Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday consumers. “Ladybird improves rapidly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust, starting with its JavaScript engine.

    While it’s exciting to have a new engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”.

    Microsoft owners are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project claims that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.

    I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the fresh KDE Plasma 6.8.3, and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.

    In a recent development, the browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without issue. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded quickly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.

    Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.

    I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.

    In a recent development, after spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most new browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.

    It has been revealed that what the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

    #116041. The loneliest peptide party in Upcoming York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1962 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

    The loneliest peptide party in Upcoming York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.
    • This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life.
    • On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.

    Photography by Jack Califano / The Verge.

    This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

    On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in New York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.

    Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The manufacturer makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.).

    Welcome to a peptide launch party.

    Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in Upcoming York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.

    According to recent reports, one person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no looks, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he said.

    The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.

    Industry observers note that A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.

    After 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.

    As it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and stated, “Giggles.”.

    If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging notes. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.

    First of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.

    In a recent development, for all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.

    According to recent reports, all that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “crucial cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.

    Recent findings suggest that if everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”.

    It has been revealed that PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.

    Recent findings suggest that another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”.

    As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.

    And good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow notes it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.

    I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.

    Not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in New York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.).

    Recent findings suggest that but a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.

    Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even declared it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.

    In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.

    In a recent development, it’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats.

    In a recent development, the feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later.

    Recent findings suggest that users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message.

    Recent findings suggest that notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos.

    Sources indicate that the feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to upgrade their teams.

    WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out.

    Just the price of its CPU, GPU and RAM goes for around $1,750.

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Due to the global RAM shortage, buying any kind of gaming gear that needs memory has gotten prohibitively expensive, which is precisely what makes this early Black Friday deal for an Alienware Aurora desktop for just $1,900 on Amazon so appealing.

    The desktop is housed in a compact 35 liter mid-tower and the system comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F processor, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB SSD and an NVIDIA RTX 5070 GPU with 12GB of vRAM. That right there is a pretty solid foundation for a mid-range gaming rig that can handle both 1080p and QHD gaming with ease (depending on the title of course). This offer is especially enticing when considering the cost of those individual components if you bought them separately.

    Industry observers note that let's start with the CPU, and compare it against other listings on Amazon. If you search for an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F, that particular CPU is actually sold out at the time of writing, and the next closest processor is a Core Ultra 7 265 processor that's going for $365. Next, we can move on to 32GB of DDR5 RAM, which is similar to this 2 x 16GB Corsair Vengeance kit that's listed for $470. Finally, there's the RTX 5070 GPU which is currently going for between $910 and $980 on Amazon from a couple different OEMs.

    Recent findings suggest that so even if we take the cheapest price for each component, you're looking at a total cost of $1,745 for just the system's three most expensive pieces of hardware, which means you're basically getting a case, a PSU, fans, heatsinks and a 1TB SSD for $150 — and without the need to do any assembly. That's one of the best deals I've seen for a gaming PC in a while. To give you even more context, if you go to the official Dell/Alienware website, you can find an Aurora desktop with the exact same specs listed at around $2,600. This means we're looking at a potential savings of around $700 compared to its standard pricing.

    Meanwhile, the rest of the system is pretty well equipped. It comes with a good selection of front IO including three USB-A, one USB-C and a 3.5mm audio jack. Around back, there's even more connectivity with a total of six additional USB connectors (two Type-C and four Type-A), 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, more audio jacks and even a SPDIF optical port. And on the inside, you get a motherboard with an Intel Z890 chipset with three PCIe slots and support for Wi-Fi 7. There's even a little window on its side panel so you can see the system's built-in RGB lighting and all those pricey components.

    However, anyone thinking about buying this system should be careful about reading too much into Amazon's listed specs. Details for this offer say the Aurora comes with a built-in optical drive, but I'm pretty sure that's a mistake. Furthermore, Amazon's page indicates the desktop comes with a 450-watt PSU, while other materials state the PC has a 500-watt power supply. Also, while you can configure an Aurora with water-cooling on Alienware's website, this particular model is merely air-cooled.

    Regardless, if you've been caught off-guard by the rapid rise in PC components over the past year and a half and have been waiting for a system with a more reasonable price, this $1,900 Alienware Aurora desktop might be the deal you're looking for. Just don't wait too long because this offer seems poised to sell out fast.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    FedEx aircraft FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway dirt in the air while overshooting Miami runway.

    The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

    Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights resumed again about 90 minutes later.

    The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.

    The ground stop came on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.

    Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.

    At 21:41 local time, the FAA confirmed that "flights will be resuming shortly".

    Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.

    "We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.

    The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.

    In a recent development, the Miami-Dade area is also under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.

    A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

    Trump indicates US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX.
    • Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX.

    Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit.

    According to recent reports, interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine.On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

    Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

    Sources indicate that in early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated, and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

    It has been revealed that in May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026.

    According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks.

    The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.

    HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is at the moment insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory.".

    Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

    According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory.

    He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

    According to recent reports, inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept.".

    "When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can right now match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

    He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian tech giant.

    He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components.".

    Recent findings suggest that "Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin noted. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being.".

    SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors.

    According to DW sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not right now require as many satellites as Starlink.

    In a recent development, ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

    But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.

    In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov stated that the number almost quadrupled.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Industry observers note that recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine.

    "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.

    Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.

    When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined.".

    Sources indicate that X announced upcoming creation tools Wednesday, many of them focused on short-form vertical video. The updates are part of the platform’s effort to compete with social networks such as YouTube and Instagram as the format continues to grow in popularity.

    The tools are designed to help creators make professional-quality vertical videos, share original content more easily, and earn more. They also give creators more ways to record, edit, and publish content directly on the platform without relying on third-party apps.

    In a recent development, A key addition is an upgraded media editor that lets creators produce polished vertical videos without leaving X. Recording features include the ability to capture video in segments and use green-screen effects, the company said.

    Sources indicate that the editor also offers a range of postproduction tools. Creators can convert horizontal videos to vertical format, automatically generate captions, trim footage, add text overlays, choose custom thumbnails, and adjust photos before publishing.

    According to recent reports, thanks to a recently announced upgrade, people can now add up to 20 photos and videos to a single post, which audiences can swipe through horizontally. X says the feature is intended for sharing event recaps, behind-the-scenes moments, and product rolls out.

    Availability of the fresh features varies by region, X said.

    Earlier this month, the manufacturer introduced a clipping feature that lets consumers take snippets from longer videos, add their own commentary, and post the clips without leaving X. Clips credit and link to the original video, plus the person who creates a clip and the original poster can earn from its views.

    Industry observers note that another feature, “React with Video,” rolled out earlier this year. Similar to TikTok’s “stitch” feature, this lets creators respond to posts with video commentary while displaying the original post in the background.

    X has also introduced upcoming earning opportunities and updates to its creator monetization programs in recent months. These include the “Video Kickstart Bonus,” an invitation-only pilot that rewards selected creators for publishing original vertical videos under three minutes long and without watermarks.

    NASA's DART mission left a stadium-sized crater in an asteroid, the ESA finds

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (359 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.
    • Recent findings suggest that in March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to new images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids.
    • Sources indicate that the crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.

    Recent findings suggest that in March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to new images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids. The 2022 controlled crash created an "impact crater the size of a sports stadium," according to Patrick Michel, the Director of Research at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Hera's principal investigator.

    Sources indicate that the crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid. Besides physically altering the surface of Dimorphos, the ESA found that the DART impact sent the asteroid tumbling in its latest orbit. Hera also revealed that both Dimorphos and Didymos are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders.

    All of these latest details were captured by Hera's monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, multi-spectral Hyperscout H and JAXA-developed Thermal Infrared Imager from about 25 to 30km away from the asteroids, the ESA says.

    "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli stated. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

    NASA and other space agencies are exploring altering asteroids' orbits as one way of protecting the Earth from potentially dangerous future impacts. In December, the ESA plans to move Hera closer to Dimorphos and Didymos to capture even higher-resolution images of the impact site. In January, Hera will also deploy shoebox-sized CubeSats to collect other types of data. The Juventas CubeSat, created by a Luxembourg-led research team, will use radar to probe the asteroid's interior and eventually land on its surface. An Italian-led team will use the other CubeSat, Milani, to prospect asteroid dust and other surrounding materials.

    #116028. The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (660 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.
    • If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
    • “The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr noted in a statement on Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

    If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

    “The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr noted in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold latest frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

    The decision, unveiled a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

    It has been revealed that this announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the tech giant wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.

    For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.

    The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The tech giant sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.

    The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The organization will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry.

    Recent findings suggest that however, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC.

    Sources indicate that half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application.

    According to recent reports, some of these environmental complications, the FCC mentioned, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket introduces, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.”.

    The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states.

    According to recent reports, as part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities.

    Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

    Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.

    The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.

    Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.

    Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.

    Recent findings suggest that beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.

    Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

    In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.

    In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.

    Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.

    King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

    While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El NiÃ±o weather pattern on record.

    Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.

    On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.

    Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.

    "Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.

    The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

    The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.

    The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.

    The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

    Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.

    Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada noted.

    King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

    Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that what happens to your private conversations when an AI manufacturer goes bankrupt?
    • Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
    • Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that what happens to your private conversations when an AI manufacturer goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the strategy is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

    Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

    Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements remarked.

    According to recent reports, only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s looks are for the chats.

    In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, Fresh York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

    “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta remarked in a statement.

    Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

    Sources indicate that “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their organization into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”.

    Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”.

    According to recent reports, the opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.).

    Recent findings suggest that character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

    California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, Fresh Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The proposed sale would include explicit conversations with children, officials say.

    Character.AI is still drawing controversy and legal scrutiny even during its bankruptcy proceedings. A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot company from auctioning off consumers' chat histories and other sensitive information.

    It has been revealed that but the auction for Character.AI won't actually safeguard people' data at all, according to the state AGs. "Character.AI's plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. "If this sale goes through, users' sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.".

    According to Bonta's office, the proposed sale includes chat histories, including conversations "in which AI characters drew children and adults into explicit sexual conversations." The buyer would also get access to chats in which users interacted with AI characters posing as physicians and therapists and discussed self harm, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts and other sensitive topics.

    The AGs have also raised concerns about the fact that only one anonymous bidder has been disclosed so far. That entity, called Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed "one day before Character.AI picked it as the base bid for the auction," and its source of funding hasn't been disclosed. "Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it," the AGs say in a court filing.

    The auction is right now scheduled for December 1. The AGs are asking the bankruptcy court to block the sale to Smirks and deny a "break-up fee" that would allow the company to collect $350,000 if Character.AI sells to another buyer. They're also asking for children's chatbot conversations and "sensitive" data to be barred from any potential sale.

    "Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder," Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said in a statement. "A company's financial troubles do not give it the right to disregard its responsibility to protect consumers, especially children.

    • Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site.
    • The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.
    • Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site.

    The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

    Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

    Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.

    On Wednesday evening, the Army noted that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.

    President Donald Trump noted shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

    "The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

    Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

    In a Wednesday evening revision on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.

    "Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added.

    Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also noted on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".

    The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

    No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.

    Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.

    He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.

    "We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.

    Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.

    The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.

    "We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.

    Sources indicate that "The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things.".

    According to recent reports, iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.

    "I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.

    It has been revealed that vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal".

    It has been revealed that illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".

    The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.

    But there is also caution from some.

    Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".

    Sand mentioned that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".

    Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, remarked there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.

    In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.

    According to recent reports, it also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.

    The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.

    But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It mentioned that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.

    Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report.

    The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

    It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to customers to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

    The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a fresh detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company states it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that customers should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

We updated our Privacy Notice to keep pace with the changing legal landscape, which increasingly requires companies to spell out how they collect and use marketing-related information. This update gives customers a clearer, more specific view of what we collect and why. These disclosures are separate from the files customers entrust to Backblaze for backup and storage, which we do not sell or share with advertisers, data brokers, or analytics partners.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the firm could get their encrypted files back.
    • Industry observers note that according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware.
    • But the organization allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the firm could get their encrypted files back.

    Industry observers note that according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The manufacturer’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”.

    But the organization allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

    Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

    The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a organization that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

    404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

    Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

    In a recent development, last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they remarked they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

    The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

    Latest Update: How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025.
    • Sources indicate that the government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous latest jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals.
    • Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 fresh data centers are located.

    Sources indicate that the government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous latest jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.

    Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, announced additional investments of $15 billion.

    "Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence, but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    According to recent reports, data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips, such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia, to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.

    According to recent reports, since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.

    In October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.

    The IFP stated that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size.".

    It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves.".

    The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.

    Sources indicate that the tech giant has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Sources indicate that in early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The firm was supposed to pay 30% upfront.

    According to recent reports, the deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.

    Recent findings suggest that in mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government swiftly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips.".

    Industry observers note that washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

    It stated that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Recent findings suggest that according to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.

    Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.

    Industry observers note that "The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

    The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.

    The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

    Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.

    Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.

    The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

    Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

    The US government also unveiled a raft of newly introduced tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

    The value of significant tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.

    But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.

    Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away.

    Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.

    Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

    "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

    Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which noted the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

    Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.

    The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.
